opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about constantly, and I'm not sure there's a single answer. My instinct has always been to show more data than people expect. There's a common assumption that you need to simplify, aggregate everything down to a few summary numbers so nobody gets overwhelmed. But the human visual system is astonishingly good at handling a lot of information at once, as long as it's organized well. People look at a dense map or a crowded city street and make sense of it immediately. So often the problem isn't too much data. It's data that hasn't been given a clear visual structure.

I usually start by asking what the viewer is actually trying to do. If they want one specific fact, say "is this number going up or down," then you strip things back and make that answer jump out. If they're exploring, trying to find something they didn't know to look for, then aggregating too early can hide exactly the thing that matters. The outliers, the weird clusters, the gaps: those are often the story, and a summary statistic smooths them away.

There's also a trick I like a lot: show everything, but at different levels of emphasis. You can put the full dataset in the background, quiet and low contrast, and then highlight the part that's relevant. That way people get the context and the focus together. They can see that the thing you're pointing at is unusual, because they can see what usual looks like.

And honestly, a lot of it is empirical. You make something, you watch people use it, and you see where they get lost or where they get bored. If they get lost, there's too much, or it isn't structured well enough. If they get bored, you've probably taken away the texture that would have made them curious. I'd almost always rather err toward richness and then work hard on the design so the richness stays legible.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the assumption that viewers need heavy simplification with the claim that people can handle a lot of information when it is well organized.

r002.rationale: It says the speaker’s instinct is to show more data than people expect and to err toward richness.

r003.rationale: For viewers seeking one specific fact, it advises stripping things back so that answer stands out.

r004.rationale: For exploration, it says viewers may be looking for something they did not know to seek, and early aggregation can hide the useful outliers, clusters, or gaps.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've been circling for most of my career, and I don't think there's a formula. But I can tell you how I think about it.

The honest answer is that the amount of data isn't really the variable I start with. I start with the question: what is this picture supposed to let someone see? And then the data question answers itself, more or less. Sometimes the right answer is enormous. When we did the Wind Map, we were showing tens of thousands of wind vectors across the entire country, and the whole point was that you couldn't summarize it. The patterns only appear when you have all of it moving at once. If you'd given me a bar chart of average wind speed by state, you'd have destroyed the thing I wanted people to feel.

Other times, the right amount is tiny. One number. I think people underrate how powerful a single well-chosen number is. The mistake I see a lot, especially from people who are technically strong, is that they treat density as a virtue in itself. More points, more dimensions, more layers. And what you end up with is something that proves you have a lot of data, but doesn't actually communicate anything.

So there's a test I use. I ask, if I remove this, does the picture get worse or better? And you'd be surprised how often removing things makes it better. Edward Tufte had this idea of data-ink ratio, and I think he was pointing at something real, although I'd put it differently. It's not about ink. It's about attention. Every mark you put on the screen is asking for a little bit of someone's attention, and attention is the actual scarce resource, not pixels.

There's also a second kind of answer that's more about honesty than clarity. Sometimes you want to show more data than is strictly needed for the main point, because showing it lets the viewer check you. If I show you a trend line and nothing else, you have to trust me. If I show you the trend line sitting on top of the raw points, you can see the noise, you can see the outliers, you can see whether I'm overstating things. So I'll often err toward showing more than the minimum, not because it adds to the message, but because it lets people argue with the message. And I think that's a healthy property for a visualization to have.

The last thing I'd say is that with interactive work, the question changes shape. You don't have to choose once. You can start with a summary and let people drill in. The TensorFlow embedding projector works this way. You see the whole cloud of points first, which is a gestalt view, and then you can zoom and select and filter down to a few neighbors. So the design question becomes less "how much do I show" and more "what's the path from overview to detail, and does each step along that path make sense."

But I'll admit that even with interactivity, you still have to decide what the first thing someone sees is. And that first frame is where most of the thinking should go.

r001.rationale: The response warns that creators may treat density as a virtue and overload viewers; it does not say people underestimate how much information viewers can handle.

r002.rationale: It recommends showing more in some cases to let viewers check a claim, but does not advise visualization beginners generally to show more data rather than less.

r003.rationale: It says to ask whether removing an element makes the picture better, and explains that extra points or layers can fail to communicate; this supports simplifying a visualization by removing information that does not serve its message.

r004.rationale: The response discusses showing raw points so viewers can inspect noise and outliers, but does not observe that one cannot know beforehand which information will be useful to them.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you want someone to be able to see. If you’re trying to communicate a particular finding, you want enough context for people to understand it and judge whether it’s convincing. But if you’re making something for exploration, you often want to show much more, because you don’t know in advance what’s going to be interesting.

And the number of data points isn’t necessarily the right measure. A million points can form a very clear pattern, while a chart with ten numbers can be confusing. The question is really: does the representation help you see structure? Can you notice the overall pattern, but also find the exceptions? That’s where interaction can be useful—you can start with the big picture and let people investigate the details.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how much data to show but does not say creators underestimate what people can handle.

r002.rationale: It says exploratory visualizations often show more, but does not advise people starting out to show more data rather than less.

r003.rationale: It recommends enough context to assess a finding, but does not say to simplify by removing data irrelevant to that point.

r004.rationale: It says that for exploration, you often show more because you do not know in advance what will be interesting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you want someone to do with it. If you’re trying to communicate a particular finding, you may want to be very selective about what you show. If you’re helping someone explore, then showing more of the data can be valuable, because you don’t know ahead of time what they’re going to notice.

The key isn’t simply the number of data points. It’s whether the viewer can make sense of what’s there. You can show a lot of data if you give it a useful structure, and you can make a very small amount of data confusing. So I’d start with the question someone is trying to answer, then think about what context they need and what detail they can explore as they go.

r001.rationale: The response says viewers can handle substantial data when it has useful structure, but does not say visualization creators tend to underestimate that capacity.

r002.rationale: It says showing more data can help exploration, but does not advise people starting to create visualizations to show more rather than less.

r003.rationale: It recommends being selective when communicating a finding, but does not specify removing data irrelevant to that finding.

r004.rationale: For exploration, it says the creator does not know in advance what viewers will notice, expressing that useful information cannot be predicted beforehand.
